		<title>How Corals Stir</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/how-corals-stir/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/how-corals-stir/#respond</comments>

		<pubDate>Thu, 06 Aug 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>

					<description><![CDATA[Reef-building coral polyps constantly stir the water around them with dense carpets of microscopic hair-like cilia. The beating of the cilia helps polyps feed while also pushing away sediment and debris. Their stirring increases nutrient and gas exchange with seawater, too. A new study combines experimental measurements with a simple mathematical model to recreate the [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Reef-building <a href="/tagged/coral/">coral</a> polyps constantly stir the water around them with dense carpets of microscopic hair-like <a href="/tagged/cilia/">cilia</a>. The beating of the cilia  helps polyps feed while also pushing away sediment and debris. Their stirring increases nutrient and gas exchange with seawater, too. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/fhfw-f1nv">A new study</a> combines experimental measurements with a simple mathematical model to recreate the three-dimensional flows corals make. The model&#8217;s efficiency means it should be useful for future studies of how corals and other cilia-covered systems interact with bacteria or other active particles. (Image and research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/fhfw-f1nv">S. Selvan et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physics.aps.org/articles/v19/76?__readwiseLocation=">APS</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" width="1024" height="643" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main-1024x643.png" alt="Particle tracks showing stirring created by coral cilia." class="wp-image-30933" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main-1024x643.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main-300x188.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main-768x482.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main-1536x965.png 1536w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/coral_stir_main.png 1936w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
]]></content:encoded>

<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/thumb1-1024x576.png" title="Putting a thumb over a hose nozzle makes the jet faster, but does it increase the flow rate?" alt="Putting a thumb over a hose nozzle makes the jet faster, but does it increase the flow rate?" /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">If you put a thumb over your hose&#8217;s outlet, you get a faster jet, but how does that affect the flow rate? That&#8217;s the question Grady starts from in this Practical Engineering video exploring <a href="/tagged/pipe-flow/">pipe flow</a> physics. 		<title>Screening for Sleep Apnea</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/screening-for-sleep-apnea/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/screening-for-sleep-apnea/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[acoustics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[aeroelastic flutter]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[biology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[machine learning]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[medicine]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[snoring]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31290</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Snoring and sleep apnea&#8211;a condition where aeroelastic flutter obstructs the airway and stops breathing during sleep&#8211;often go hand-in-hand. But diagnosing sleep apnea involves an expensive and time-consuming screening in which the patient has to sleep while monitored by various sensors. To make the process easier, researchers are developing a screening method based only on audio [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Snoring and sleep apnea&#8211;a condition where <a href="/tagged/aeroelastic-flutter">aeroelastic flutter</a> obstructs the airway and stops breathing during sleep&#8211;often go hand-in-hand. But diagnosing sleep apnea involves an expensive and time-consuming screening in which the patient has to sleep while monitored by various sensors. To make the process easier, researchers are <a href="https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6579/ae6f6a">developing a screening method</a> based only on audio recording. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">They started with a pre-trained audio model designed for speech recognition and stripped back computationally-expensive layers that weren&#8217;t relevant to snoring. Then they trained the new model using labeled audio data taken from standard clinical testing for sleep apnea. That means the model was told which audio recordings corresponded to &#8220;normal&#8221; snoring and which showed signs of sleep apnea. From there, the model was able to correctly identify apnea-related audio from fresh recordings just under 74% of the time. While that accuracy isn&#8217;t high enough to use the tool for diagnosis, it could help patients pre-screen for sleep apnea at home to decide whether the more invasive testing is warranted. (Image credit: <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/2-children-lying-on-bed-ClqFQz8RNKA">L. Cline</a>; research credit: <a href="https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6579/ae6f6a">H. Li et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physicsworld.com/a/abnormal-snoring-sounds-help-diagnose-common-sleep-disorder/">Physics World</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Microplastics in the Water Column</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/microplastics-in-the-water-column/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/08/microplastics-in-the-water-column/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 03 Aug 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[buoyancy]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[microplastics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[oceanography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[pollution]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31688</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Of the more than 9 billion metric tons of plastic that&#8217;s been produced, a mere 9% has been recycled. About 12% has been incinerated, and the remainder is just out there&#8211;in our homes, our landfills, and, unfortunately, in our oceans. Exactly where all the plastic is continues to be an active question of research. Plastic&#8217;s [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Of the more than 9 billion metric tons of plastic that&#8217;s been produced, a mere 9% has been recycled. About 12% has been incinerated, and the remainder is just out there&#8211;in our homes, our landfills, and, unfortunately, in our oceans. Exactly <em>where</em> all the plastic is continues to be an <a href="https://eos.org/features/measuring-microplastics-in-every-ocean-layer?__readwiseLocation=">active question of research</a>. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Plastic&#8217;s density is similar to that of water; some versions are a little denser than water, and some are a little lighter. So whether a piece of plastic floats at the ocean surface or sinks to the bottom depends on several factors, including its density, size, and shape. A large, dense plastic&#8211;think laundry detergent bottles&#8211;can float if it displaces enough water; after all, metal ships float! </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">But as sunlight and abrasion breaks that big container into smaller fragments, their <a href="/tagged/buoyancy">buoyancy</a> shrinks. Eventually, these small, millimetric pieces sink, carrying our pollution to ecosystems we once thought remote. Some of the highest rates of microplastic ingestion are found in <a href="https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/lno.12370">nonmigratory species living between 1200 and 1500 meters</a> below the surface. We may never visit those depths, but our garbage does. (Image credit: <a href="https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/plastic-pollution-micro-nurdles-and-plastic-particle-in-ocean-water-gm1184974030-333767639?searchscope=image%2Cfilm">iStock/dottedhippo</a>; via <a href="https://eos.org/features/measuring-microplastics-in-every-ocean-layer?__readwiseLocation=">Eos</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<item>
		<title>Ice Giant or Magma Ocean World?</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/ice-giant-or-magma-ocean-world/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/ice-giant-or-magma-ocean-world/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[geophysics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[magma]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[miscibility]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[numerical simulation]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[planetary science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[supercritical fluids]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31585</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Uranus and Neptune&#8211;known as our system&#8217;s ice giants&#8211;are our least explored planets. Both have received exactly one flyby, from the Voyager 2 spacecraft. The data from those flybys remain our primary source of knowledge about each planet. The traditional model for each planet&#8217;s interior (dating back to before the flybys) consists of three layers: a [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="/tagged/uranus/">Uranus</a> and <a href="/tagged/neptune/">Neptune</a>&#8211;known as our system&#8217;s ice giants&#8211;are our least explored planets. Both have received exactly one flyby, from the Voyager 2 spacecraft. The data from those flybys remain our primary source of knowledge about each planet. The traditional model for each planet&#8217;s interior (dating back to before the flybys) consists of three layers: a rocky core; an icy mantle made up of water, ammonia, and methane; and a hydrogen/helium-rich atmosphere. That structure is one way to match the limited measurements we have from these planets, but, as today&#8217;s <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18219">preprint study</a> points out, it&#8217;s not the only way. </p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The authors suggest an alternative structure, in which a hydrogen-rich atmosphere overlays a <a href="/tagged/supercritical-fluids/">supercritical</a> magma ocean capable of dissolving hydrogen into heavier, metallic elements. Their suggestion is motivated by several factors. First, objects in the outer solar system&#8211;including Kuiper Belt objects&#8211;have less icy material than originally assumed, which suggests that Uranus and Neptune&#8217;s progenitors wouldn&#8217;t have been so ice-rich, either. Second, our understanding of how &#8220;rocky&#8221; materials respond at the temperatures and pressures found in these planet interiors has evolved. In particular, silicate, hydrogen, and iron are actually <a href="/tagged/miscibility/">miscible</a> at these conditions. That means that discrete sub-layers separated by material type are <em>not</em> as likely.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Using the magma ocean model, the team found compositions for both Uranus and Neptune that conformed well to our limited data about their gravitational and magnetic field properties. Time&#8211;and more data&#8211;will tell as to which interior model best describes these enigmatic giants. (Image credit: <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/uranus-planet-Li41RApUAQA">NASA</a>; research credit: <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18219">E. Young et al.</a> (preprint); via <a href="https://gizmodo.com/scientists-think-uranus-and-neptune-may-not-be-the-ice-giants-we-imagined-2000778382?__readwiseLocation=">Gizmodo</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>
					
					<wfw:commentRss>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/ice-giant-or-magma-ocean-world/feed/</wfw:commentRss>

		<item>
		<title>Giant Water Balloon to the Face</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/giant-water-balloon-to-the-face/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/giant-water-balloon-to-the-face/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 29 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Phenomena]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[inertia]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[surface tension]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[water balloons]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=31603</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[It&#8217;s the summertime, so Gav and Dan of the Slow Mo Guys are back to experimenting with giant water balloons. In this video, they send several careening down a slope into Dan&#8217;s face. Watching the balloons descend and pop is (unsurprisingly) my favorite part. It&#8217;s neat to see how the elasticity of the balloon acts [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<div class="wp-block-envira-envira-gallery"><div class="envira-gallery-feed-output"><img decoding="async" class="envira-gallery-feed-image" tabindex="0" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/balloon_face1-1024x576.png" title="The water blob is coming..." alt="The water blob is coming..." /></div></div>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">It&#8217;s the summertime, so Gav and Dan of the Slow Mo Guys are back to experimenting with giant water balloons. In this video, they send   several careening down a slope into Dan&#8217;s face. Watching the balloons descend and pop is (unsurprisingly) my favorite part. It&#8217;s neat to see how the <a href="/tagged/elasticity/">elasticity</a> of the balloon acts like a beefed-up <a href="/tagged/surface-tension/">surface tension</a> to make this enormous blob of water act like an oversized droplet. (Video and image credit: The Slow Mo Guys)</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph"></p>

		<title>Inside an Espresso Bed</title>
		<link>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/inside-an-espresso-bed/</link>
					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/inside-an-espresso-bed/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Nicole Sharp]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Research]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[coffee]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[espresso]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[flow visualization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[fluid dynamics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[physics]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[porous media]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[porous medium]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[science]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://fyfluiddynamics.com/?p=30959</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[When pulling a shot of espresso, there are complicated physics at play. The ground coffee is tamped into a puck-like bed of grains, through which high-temperature, high-pressure water is forced. Here, researchers used X-ray tomography to visualize how and when water moves through the bed, which affects how flavors extract. In a finely ground bed, [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">When pulling a shot of <a href="/tagged/coffee/">espresso</a>, there are complicated physics at play. The ground coffee is tamped into a puck-like bed of grains, through which high-temperature, high-pressure water is forced. Here, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">researchers used</a> X-ray tomography to <a href="/tagged/flow-visualization/">visualize</a> how and when water moves through the bed, which affects how flavors extract.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img decoding="async" width="1024" height="496" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-1024x496.png" alt="Composite images of water penetrating a bed of finely ground coffee (left) and a bed of coarsely ground coffee (right)." class="wp-image-30960" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-1024x496.png 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-300x145.png 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1-768x372.png 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/2026-04-allen-coffee-fig2-1.png 1200w" sizes="(max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /><figcaption class="wp-element-caption">Composite images of water penetrating a bed of finely ground coffee (left) and a bed of coarsely ground coffee (right).</figcaption></figure>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">In a finely ground bed, water is relatively slow to penetrate the bed, but moves in fairly uniformly. Water can get into the coarse grind a little faster but does so less uniformly. With the new experimental technique in place, the team is interested in seeing how water temperature affects infiltration and what solids get extracted. (Image credit: top &#8211; <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/white-ceramic-mug-with-coffee-CbBY9Q9m4fY">R. Wicks</a>, experiment &#8211; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">J. Foster et al.</a>; research credit: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0245167">J. Foster et al.</a>; via <a href="https://physicsworld.com/a/coffee-with-a-splash-of-physics-how-to-make-the-most-out-of-your-brew/?nbd_source=3626823&amp;__readwiseLocation=">Physics World</a>)</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Canyon Swirls</title>

					<comments>https://fyfluiddynamics.com/2026/07/canyon-swirls/#respond</comments>

					<description><![CDATA[For much of the year, Cañon Fiord in the Canadian Arctic lies under ice and snow, but in the summer melt season, colors peek out. Here sea ice and sediment swirl in the fjord in eddies that are kilometers wide. The sediment is largely glacial flour&#8211;rock that&#8217;s been ground into dust by glaciers. It provides [&#8230;]]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">For much of the year, Cañon Fiord in the Canadian Arctic lies under ice and snow, but in the summer melt season, colors peek out. Here sea ice and sediment swirl in the fjord in eddies that are kilometers wide. The sediment is largely glacial flour&#8211;rock that&#8217;s been ground into dust by glaciers. It provides critical nutrients  for the marine ecosystem. (Image credit: L. Dauphin; via <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/canon-fiords-whirling-waters/?__readwiseLocation=">NASA Earth Observatory</a>)</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image aligncenter size-large"><img loading="lazy" decoding="async" width="1024" height="683" src="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-1024x683.jpg" alt="Satellite image of sea ice and sediment swirling in Cañon Fiord." class="wp-image-30688" srcset="https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-1024x683.jpg 1024w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-300x200.jpg 300w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main-768x512.jpg 768w, https://fyfluiddynamics.com/wp-content/uploads/ellesmereislandwide_main.jpg 1440w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px" /></figure>
